content.introduction: The bull market faces a new challenge as capital becomes more expensive due to the AI buildout's unprecedented demand for money. The stock market is influenced by the enormous capital demand for AI infrastructure, data centers, power generation, and the electric grid. Despite this, investors have more choices today than before, with global markets becoming more competitive, bonds offering meaningful income, and diversification potentially providing benefits. While there is concern about interest rate hikes potentially ending the bull market, history suggests that such risks may not derail it due to economic and corporate earnings growth. Technology stocks, especially semiconductors, are expected to remain attractive due to robust earnings growth. The market continues to reach new highs thanks to accelerating profit growth, renewed excitement over AI, and a resilient job market.
body:
The bull market has a new problem: Capital is becoming more expensive just as the AI buildout requires unprecedented amounts of it.

### What’s influencing the stock market right now? [...] The enormous demand for capital adds another dimension. We have never had a technological revolution this hungry for money. AI infrastructure, data centers, power generation, and the electric grid all require substantial investment, and hyperscalers are raising enormous sums to finance that buildout. [...] The good news is that investors have more choices today than they did a few years ago. The world is your oyster. Global markets have become more competitive, bonds once again offer meaningful income, and diversification may provide benefits that were harder to appreciate when a small group of large US technology stocks dominated returns. Read _Viewpoints:_The new diversification

Stocks have been volatile in recent weeks amid new developments on geopolitics and interest rates, though business fundamentals have continued to show strength.
   Some investors fear there is one big risk that could finally stop this extended bull market: interest rate hikes.
   History shows Fed rate hikes don't always have to hurt stocks. Periods of tightening have often accompanied stronger economic growth and periods of rising stock prices. [...] As we look ahead to the second half, investors face potential risks, including the potential for rate hikes designed to tame inflation.
   History suggests those risks may not be enough to derail a bull market that’s been fueled by economic and corporate earnings growth.
   Technology stocks, particularly semiconductors, should remain attractive as the sector’s robust earnings growth is likely to continue. [...] Recent market volatility has raised fresh questions about how much longer this extended bull market can run. Even as exceptional earnings growth has powered stocks to record highs this year, investors have grappled with a mounting list of concerns, from higher oil prices and geopolitical tensions to the possibility of higher interest rates.

Of those risks, the specter of rate hikes has remained the one big risk that many investors fear could end this extended bull market.

Topics covered:
• This 2026 Midyear Outlook webinar breaks down whether the bull market can continue, with expert insights on stocks, bonds, inflation, interest rates, and the impact of AI on the economy.
• Fidelity leaders explore key investment trends, Federal Reserve policy, and diversification strategies, to help investors navigate potential opportunities and risks in the second half of 2026. [...] ### Transcript
[0:00] Hello there, everybody, and thank you so much for joining us for this special in-person edition of Market Sense. I'm Heather Hegedus, with Fidelity.
[0:08] And we are coming to you midway through the year, where the headline is an economy that seems to be firing on all cylinders.
[0:15] And the stock market continues to reach new all-time highs.
[0:18] And that is thanks to accelerating profit growth, renewed excitement over AI, and a pretty resilient job market. [...] [29:29] We have data that cover over 200 years of technological transformations-- to your point, the personal computer, steam railways, electricity.
[29:39] And there's a pattern that's actually pretty consistent across all of those. And it's three factors.
[29:45] And basically, the first thing that happens-- stock prices go up because they get excited about the new technology. And we're there, right? So we're there. Mark is excited about it.
